# 2. Clustering and annotation

**Module 02 — Clustering and annotation.** Normalize, cluster, and annotate cells. Run module `01` first, or run the setup chunk below in a new session after module `01` checkpoints exist. **Decision checkpoint** callouts cover clustering parameters, manual labels, and optional CD4 gating examples below.

```{r}
#| label: module02_setup

library(here)
here::i_am("pna_3/modules/02_clustering_annotation.qmd")

source(here::here("pna_3", "modules", "common_setup.R"))

if (!exists("pg_data", inherits = TRUE)) {
  pg_data <- load_checkpoint("pg_data_merged.rds")
}
if (!exists("selected_markers", inherits = TRUE)) {
  selected_markers <- load_checkpoint("selected_markers.rds")
}

set.seed(analysis_seed)
```

## 2.1. Normalize and scale data

Cells failing QC were removed in module `01`. The checkpoint `pg_data_merged.rds` contains the filtered object only.

PNA data are normalized using centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation over margin 2, which normalizes counts per cell by dividing by the geometric mean across all markers for that cell. This normalization approach effectively accounts for differences in sequencing depth between cells while preserving the relative differences in marker abundance within each cell. The CLR transformation is particularly well-suited for compositional data like PNA, where the total signal per cell can vary substantially.

Following normalization, the data are Z-score scaled per marker. This transformation centers each marker's distribution around zero and scales it to unit variance. Z-score scaling is essential for downstream dimensionality reduction and clustering analyses, as it ensures that all markers contribute equally to the analysis regardless of their absolute abundance levels. Without this scaling step, highly abundant markers would dominate the analysis, potentially obscuring important signals from less abundant but biologically relevant markers.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_normalize_scale

pg_data <-
  pg_data |>
  NormalizeData(normalization.method = "CLR", margin = 2) |>
  ScaleData()
```

## 2.2. Dimensionality reduction

> **Decision checkpoint** (PCA / UMAP hyperparameters)\
> In the next chunk, adjust `n_pcs` (how many PCs `RunPCA` computes), `n_dims` (how many of those feed `RunUMAP` and clustering) and `n_neighbors` to match your dataset; use the PCA elbow plot to choose `n_dims`. `RunPCA(..., features = selected_markers)` uses the marker list from module `01`.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is performed to extract the main axes of variation in the data. The first 10-20 principal components (PCs) are typically used for downstream analysis, though this number should be adjusted based on the specific dataset and experimental design. As a general guideline, the selected PCs should explain a substantial portion of the total variance while avoiding overfitting to noise. Principal components often capture technical effects, cell states, or experimental conditions, so the number of PCs can be adjusted according to the expected number of cell states or the complexity of the experimental design. The number of PCs is set to 20 by default, but can be adjusted as needed.

If marker selection was performed in the Quality Control section, those selected markers can be used for PCA instead of all markers. This optional step helps reduce noise from low-abundance or non-informative markers and can improve the interpretability of the results.

Following PCA, Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is applied to visualize the data in a two-dimensional space. UMAP is a non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that preserves both local neighborhood structure and global relationships in the data. This makes it particularly well-suited for visualizing complex single-cell PNA datasets, where it can reveal cell type clusters and relationships that may not be apparent in higher-dimensional space. The number of neighbors is set to 30 by default, but can be adjusted as needed.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_dimensionality_reduction

# n_pcs: how many principal components RunPCA computes (kept generous so the
#        elbow plot below has range to inspect).
# n_dims: how many of those are actually used for UMAP and clustering.
n_pcs <- 50
n_dims <- 10 #20 # DECISION POINT
n_neighbors <- 30 # DECISION POINT
pg_data <-
  pg_data |>
  RunPCA(npcs = n_pcs, features = selected_markers, seed.use = analysis_seed) |>
  RunUMAP(
    reduction = "pca",
    dims = 1:n_dims,
    n.neighbors = n_neighbors,
    seed.use = analysis_seed
  ) # EDITED: Fix in PAT

pca_red <-
  Reductions(pg_data, "pca")

pca_red@stdev |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "PC") |>
  mutate(
    PC = PC |>
      str_remove("PC_") |>
      as.integer()
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(PC, value)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point() +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "PCA Elbow Plot",
    x = "Principal Component",
    y = "Standard Deviation"
  )
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/dimensionality_reduction_plots/data_processing_pca_elbow_plot"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)

cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(pg_data, c("sample_alias", "condition")) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

Embeddings(pg_data, "pca") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(PC_1, PC_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/dimensionality_reduction_plots/data_processing_pca"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)


Embeddings(pg_data, "umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(umap_1, umap_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/dimensionality_reduction_plots/data_processing_umap"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)
```

## 2.3. Data harmonization

> **Decision checkpoint** (batch integration)\
> If you use Harmony, set `group.by.vars` to the metadata column that defines batches (often `"sample_alias"`). If you **skip** Harmony, do not run the chunk below. In the clustering chunk below, change `reduction = "harmony"` to `reduction = "pca"` and `reduction.name = "harmony_umap"` to `"umap"`, then use `"pca"` / `"umap"` instead of `"harmony"` / `"harmony_umap"` in later plots.

Data harmonization is an optional step that can be beneficial when experiments contain multiple samples with similar cell types that do not cluster together well due to technical or biological variability. The goal of data harmonization is to align similar cell types across samples so that they cluster together, facilitating the identification of shared cell types between samples even when they exhibit somewhat different protein expression profiles. This approach is particularly useful in experiments with batch effects, technical variability, or biological sources of variation such as donor differences or stimulation-induced perturbations.

The Harmony algorithm is used here to harmonize the data based on sample ID, though any sample metadata column can be specified for harmonization. The algorithm integrates information across samples while preserving biological variation within each sample.

**Important considerations**: Users should carefully inspect the harmonized data to ensure that harmonization has not removed important biological variation and that similar cell types are indeed clustering together across samples. In many cases, harmonization is not necessary, particularly when samples are already well-mixed and similar cell types cluster together naturally without harmonization.

The harmonization process generates a new dimensional reduction called "harmony", which is used for UMAP visualization and clustering. Importantly, the original data remains unchanged, so harmonization is used primarily to identify common cell identities across samples rather than to modify the underlying expression data.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_data_harmonization
pg_data <-
  pg_data |>
  RunHarmony(
    group.by.vars = "sample_alias", # DECISION POINT
    plot_convergence = FALSE
  ) |>
  RunUMAP(
    reduction = "harmony",
    dims = 1:n_dims,
    reduction.name = "harmony_umap",
    n.neighbors = n_neighbors,
    seed.use = analysis_seed
  )

cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(pg_data, c("sample_alias", "condition")) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmony_1, harmony_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/dimensionality_reduction_plots/data_processing_harmony"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)

Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony_umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/dimensionality_reduction_plots/data_processing_harmonyumap"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)
```

## 2.4. Clustering

> **Decision checkpoint** (clustering graph and resolution)\
> In the next chunk, tune `FindNeighbors` (`reduction`, `dims`) and `FindClusters(..., resolution = ...)`. Try a few resolutions and compare UMAP/cluster plots.

Clustering groups cells with similar protein expression profiles into discrete clusters, which can subsequently be annotated as distinct cell types or cell states. This step is essential for identifying and characterizing the cellular composition of the dataset.

Leiden clustering is performed on a k-nearest neighbor graph constructed from the dimensionality-reduced space (either PCA or Harmony reduction). The algorithm identifies communities of cells that are more densely connected to each other than to cells in other communities, effectively partitioning the data into biologically meaningful groups.

The resolution parameter is a critical hyperparameter that controls the granularity of the clustering. Higher resolution values result in more fine-grained clusters (more clusters with fewer cells each), while lower values produce broader clusters (fewer clusters with more cells each). The optimal resolution depends on the dataset characteristics, experimental design, and the level of cellular heterogeneity expected. Users should test multiple resolution values (e.g., 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 1.0) and visually inspect the resulting clusters on UMAP plots to determine which resolution best captures the expected cell type diversity without over-clustering or under-clustering the data. The resolution is set to 0.5 by default, but can be adjusted as needed.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_clustering
# (clustering uses the same n_dims as the UMAP above)
pg_data <-
  pg_data |>
  FindNeighbors(reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:n_dims) |>
  FindClusters(random.seed = analysis_seed, resolution = 0.5) # DECISION POINT

cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(pg_data, c("sample_alias", "condition", "seurat_clusters")) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmony_1, harmony_2, color = seurat_clusters)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cluster_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/clustering_plots/data_processing_harmony_clusters"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)

Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony_umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = seurat_clusters)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cluster_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/clustering_plots/data_processing_harmonyumap_clusters"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)
```

## 2.5. Marker Distribution on UMAP

This section visualizes the distribution of markers of interest on the harmonized UMAP. This can help to identify which markers are characteristic of each cluster, and can guide manual annotation of cell types.

> **Decision checkpoint** (markers for FeaturePlots)\
> Set `markers_of_interest` in the next chunk to the markers you want on UMAP for annotation (independent from the abundance heatmap section unless you choose to align them).

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_marker_distribution_on_umap

markers_of_interest <-
  c(
    "CD3e",
    "CD4",
    "CD8",
    "CD19",
    "CD56",
    "CD14",
    "CD16",
    "HLA-DR",
    "CD11c",
    "CD123",
    "FMC63"
  )

for (marker in markers_of_interest) {
  feature_plot <- FeaturePlot(
    pg_data,
    features = marker,
    reduction = "harmony_umap"
  ) &
    theme(aspect.ratio = 1)

  savename_marker <- str_remove_all(marker, "\\.") # remove dots from marker names for saving
  export_plot(
    filename = glue::glue(here::here(
      "pna_3",
      "results/02_clustering_annotation/marker_umap_plots/{savename_marker}_umap"
    )),
    plot = feature_plot,
    width = 6,
    height = 6
  )
}
```

## 2.6. Annotation

### 2.6.1. Automatic annotation

Automatic cell annotation is performed by matching each cell's protein expression profile to annotated cells in a reference peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) dataset using label transfer methods. This approach provides an initial annotation framework that can accelerate the annotation process.

**Important limitations and recommendations**: Automated annotations should be interpreted with caution, particularly when the sample composition differs substantially from the PBMC reference dataset. For example, annotations may be unreliable for certain stimulated samples, cell lines, or tissues that are not well-represented in the reference. Additionally, automated methods may not capture cell states or subtypes that are specific to the experimental conditions.

All automated annotations should be inspected, verified, and adjusted as necessary. Automated annotation serves as a starting point, but manual review and refinement are essential to ensure accurate and context-appropriate cell type assignments. Users should carefully examine marker expression patterns, differential abundance results, and UMAP visualizations to validate and refine the automated annotations before proceeding with downstream analyses.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_annotation

# Load reference dataset
reference <- pixelatorR::read_pbmc_reference()

# Set names of annotation columns in reference
reference$l1_annotation <- reference$celltype.l1
reference$l2_annotation <- reference$celltype.l2

# Annotation by label transfer
pg_data <-
  pg_data |>
  AnnotateCells(
    reference = reference,
    reference_groups = c("l1_annotation", "l2_annotation"),
    reference_assay = "PNA",
    query_assay = "PNA",
    # Summarise annotations by cluster, adding an extra column with majority vote
    summarize_by_column = "seurat_clusters",
    normalization_method = "CLR",
    method = "nmf"
  )


cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data,
    c(
      "sample_alias",
      "condition",
      "seurat_clusters",
      "l1_annotation_summary",
      "l2_annotation_summary",
      "l1_annotation",
      "l2_annotation"
    )
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

# L1 automatic annotation - summarised by cluster
Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony_umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = l1_annotation_summary)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>%
      group_by(l1_annotation_summary) %>%
      summarise(
        harmonyumap_1 = median(harmonyumap_1),
        harmonyumap_2 = median(harmonyumap_2)
      ),
    aes(label = l1_annotation_summary),
    size = 3,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/automatic_annotation/data_processing_harmonyumap_l1_annotation_summary"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)


# L1 automatic annotation - annotated by cell
Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony_umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = l1_annotation)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>%
      group_by(l1_annotation) %>%
      summarise(
        harmonyumap_1 = median(harmonyumap_1),
        harmonyumap_2 = median(harmonyumap_2)
      ),
    aes(label = l1_annotation),
    size = 3,
    color = "black"
  ) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cell_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/automatic_annotation/data_processing_harmonyumap_l1_annotation"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 4
)


# L2 automatic annotation - summarised by cluster
Embeddings(pg_data, "harmony_umap") |>

  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
```

### 2.6.2. Discover Cell Types

While automated annotation provides a useful starting point, manual inspection and refinement are essential to ensure accuracy. This section performs differential abundance analysis to identify cluster-specific marker expression patterns, which serve as the foundation for manual cell type identification.

Differential abundance analysis compares marker expression levels between each cluster and all other clusters, identifying markers that are significantly enriched or depleted in specific clusters. These cluster-specific markers are characteristic features that can be used to identify cell types based on known marker expression patterns. For example, clusters enriched for CD3, CD4, and CD45RA are likely CD4+ T cells, while clusters showing high CD19 and CD20 expression are likely B cells.

The analysis generates two key visualizations to aid interpretation:

1.  **Heatmap of differential abundance**: Displays the average CLR difference for each marker across all clusters, allowing rapid identification of which markers distinguish each cluster. Markers with strong positive values (red) are enriched in that cluster, while negative values (blue) indicate depletion. This overview helps identify clusters with similar marker profiles and those with unique expression signatures.

2.  **Volcano plots per cluster**: Show the relationship between statistical significance and effect size for each marker within each cluster. Markers in the upper right or upper left quadrants (high significance and large effect size) are the most reliable cluster-defining markers. The top markers for each cluster are automatically labeled, facilitating quick identification of key distinguishing features.

By examining these differential abundance patterns in conjunction with known cell type marker expression profiles, users can systematically identify cell types. The process involves: (1) identifying clusters with characteristic marker combinations, (2) comparing these patterns to established cell type markers, (3) confirming or adjusting automated annotations based on the observed expression patterns, and (4) identifying cell populations that may not be well-represented in the reference dataset. This evidence-based approach complements automated annotation and significantly improves confidence in cell type assignments.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_manual_annotation

diff_abundant_markers_cluster <-
  FindAllMarkers(
    pg_data,
    logfc.threshold = 0,
    # NOTE: the argument is min.pct, not min_pct - an unmatched name falls into
    # `...` and is silently ignored, leaving the default min.pct = 0.01 in place.
    min.pct = 0,
    # return.thresh defaults to 0.01, which caps the returned table at
    # p_val < 0.01. Set to 1 so the volcano plot below shows the full
    # significance range rather than only the significant tail.
    return.thresh = 1,
    test.use = "wilcox",
    assay = "PNA",
    slot = "data",
    group.by = "seurat_clusters",
    mean.fxn = rowMeans,
    fc.name = "difference"
  ) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  rename(marker = gene)

# Heatmap of differential abundance markers per cluster
diff_abundant_markers_cluster |>
  group_by(marker) |>
  filter(any(p_val_adj < 0.05 & difference > 1)) |>
  select(marker, difference, cluster) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = cluster,
    values_from = difference,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  column_to_rownames("marker") |>
  t() |>
  pheatmap(
    color = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry"),
    breaks = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 101),
    cellwidth = 8,
    cellheight = 8,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "CLR Difference")
  ) |>
  as.ggplot()
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/cluster_specific_markers/data_processing_differential_abundance_markers_per_cluster"
  ),
  width = 14,
  height = 5
)

# Volcano plot of differential abundance markers per cluster.
diff_abundant_markers_cluster |>
  mutate(neg_log10_p_val = -log10(pmax(p_val_adj, min_p_value_threshold))) |>
  ggplot(aes(difference, neg_log10_p_val, color = difference)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), col = "grey") +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>%
      group_by(cluster) %>%
      slice_max(abs(difference), n = 5),
    aes(label = marker),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 2
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~cluster) +
  scale_color_gradientn(
    colors = gradient_palette,
    limits = c(-1, 1) *
      max(abs(diff_abundant_markers_cluster$difference), na.rm = TRUE)
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Differential abundance markers per cluster",
    x = "Average CLR Difference",
    y = "-log10(Adj. p value)",
    color = "Effect size"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
```

### 2.6.4. Set manual annotation

> **Decision checkpoint** (manual cell type labels — critical for biology)\
> Replace the `cluster_cell_annotation` named vector in the next chunk so every `seurat_clusters` level in your data has a label. Add or remove cluster keys if your resolution differs from the example.

In this step we assign cell type labels to each cluster based on the analysis performed in the previous sections. Annotations should be informed by a combination of differential abundance results, marker abundance patterns, automated predictions, and known biology, as well as experiment context.

Clusters are mapped to cell types using a named vector. Multiple clusters can share the same label if they represent different states or subtypes of the same cell type (e.g., several clusters annotated as “CD4 T”).

The example annotations provided here are placeholders. You should review the available evidence and adapt them to your dataset before proceeding. Alternatively, if you wish to use the automatic annotations without modification, you can skip this step and e.g. use the `l1_annotation_summary` column for downstream analyses instead of `manual_cell_annotation`.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_set_manual_annotation

# Inspect the automatic annotation results to inform manual annotation
# The `l1_annotation` and `l2_annotation` columns contain the automatic annotation per each individual cell,
# while `l1_annotation_summary` and `l2_annotation_summary` contain the majority vote annotation per cluster

# This plot shows the distribution of automatic annotations across clusters,
# which can help to identify which clusters correspond to which cell types,
# and to identify whether the clustering resolves all cell identities of interest.

# Cell counts per cluster
table(pg_data$seurat_clusters, pg_data$l2_annotation_summary) %>% # DECISION POINT: select annotation level to compare with
  ComplexHeatmap::pheatmap(
    .,
    color = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry"),
    display_numbers = ifelse(. == 0, "", .),
    cellwidth = 16,
    cellheight = 8,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "Number of cells")
  ) |>
  as.ggplot()
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/cluster_vs_automatic_annotation/cluster_vs_l2_annotation_summary_counts"
  ),
  width = 10,
  height = 6
)

table(pg_data$seurat_clusters, pg_data$l2_annotation_summary) %>%
  sweep(1, rowSums(.), FUN = "/") %>%
  `*`(100) %>% # Multiply by 100
  round(1) %>%
  ComplexHeatmap::pheatmap(
    .,
    color = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry"),
    display_numbers = ifelse(. == 0, "", .),
    cellwidth = 16,
    cellheight = 8,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "% of cells")
  ) |>
  as.ggplot()
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/cluster_vs_automatic_annotation/cluster_vs_l2_annotation_summary_percent"
  ),
  width = 10,
  height = 6
)

# Specify cell annotation labels for each cluster
# (These are example annotations and should be changed according to your dataset)
cell_anno_df <- table(
  pg_data$seurat_clusters,
  pg_data$l2_annotation_summary # DECISION POINT: select level to base annotation on
) %>%
  sweep(1, rowSums(.), FUN = "/") %>%
  `*`(100) %>% # Multiply by 100
  round(1)

# This relies on the *_annotation_summary column being a per-cluster majority
# vote, so every cluster row is 100% one label. If that does not hold, apply()
# returns a list of varying lengths and the indexing below fails obscurely.
n_hits <- apply(cell_anno_df, 1, function(x) sum(x == 100))
if (any(n_hits != 1)) {
  stop(
    "Expected exactly one 100% annotation per cluster, but cluster(s) ",
    paste(rownames(cell_anno_df)[n_hits != 1], collapse = ", "),
    " matched ",
    paste(n_hits[n_hits != 1], collapse = ", "),
    ". Use an *_annotation_summary column, which is constant within a cluster."
  )
}

cluster_cell_annotation <- setNames(
  colnames(cell_anno_df)[apply(cell_anno_df, 1, function(x) which(x == 100))],
  rownames(cell_anno_df)
)

# NOTE: recode() drops names, so the setNames() below is load-bearing - it
# re-attaches the cluster ids by position. Do not remove it.
cluster_cell_annotation <- cluster_cell_annotation |>
  recode(
    "CD4 TEM" = "CD4 T",
    "Naive CD4 T" = "CD4 T",
    "CD8 TCM" = "CD8 T",
    "Naive CD8 T" = "CD8 T",
    "Classical Mono" = "Myeloid",
    "Non-classical Mono" = "Myeloid",
    "DC" = "Myeloid",
    "CD56dim NK" = "NK",
    "Treg" = "T other",
    "gdT" = "T other"
  ) |>
  setNames(nm = rownames(cell_anno_df))

# Add annotation to Seurat object
pg_data[[]] <-
  pg_data[[]] |>
  mutate(
    manual_cell_annotation = cluster_cell_annotation[as.character(
      seurat_clusters
    )]
  )
```

The FMC63+ split is not made at the cluster level here — clustering does not
separate FMC63 status cleanly enough. It is done by marker gating in section
2.6.6 below.

### 2.6.6. Alternative: Marker gating

> **Optional path**\
> Use this section only if you want gating-based annotation; gate coordinates and marker pairs must match **your** CLR distributions.

Marker gating provides an alternative approach to cell annotation that is analogous to flow cytometry gating strategies. This method uses density scatter plots to visualize the co-expression of two markers, allowing users to identify distinct cell populations based on marker expression patterns and define gates (thresholds) to classify cells.

The `DensityScatterPlot()` function creates a two-dimensional density plot showing the relationship between two markers, where each axis represents the expression level (typically CLR-normalized values) of one marker. Dense regions in the plot represent cell populations with similar marker expression profiles, while sparse regions indicate transitions between populations or rare cell types.

**How to use marker gating for annotation:**

1.  **Select marker pairs**: Choose pairs of markers that are known to distinguish cell types of interest. For example:

    - CD3e vs CD4: Distinguishes T cells (CD3e+) and CD4+ T cells (CD3e+ CD4+)
    - CD3e vs CD8: Distinguishes T cells and CD8+ T cells
    - CD19 vs CD20: Identifies B cells
    - CD14 vs CD16: Distinguishes monocyte subsets

2.  **Visualize marker pairs**: Generate density scatter plots for relevant marker combinations to identify distinct cell populations and their expression boundaries.

3.  **Define gates**: Based on the density patterns, identify threshold values for each marker that separate different cell populations. These thresholds can be used to classify cells into categories.

4.  **Apply gates to clusters**: Use the identified marker expression thresholds to validate or refine cluster annotations. Clusters that don't match expected marker expression patterns may need re-examination.

5.  **Compare with other annotation methods**: Cross-reference gating-based annotations with automated annotation results, differential abundance analysis, and UMAP visualizations to ensure consistency.

This gating approach is particularly useful for validating annotations, identifying misclassified clusters, and understanding marker expression relationships. It complements the cluster-based annotation approach by providing a marker-centric perspective on cell type identification.

Below is an example of how to use the gating strategy to annotate CD4 T cell subtypes.

#### 2.6.6.1 Gating T cells based on FMC63 status

Let's first view the distribution of FMC63 in the T cell populations split based on the cluster-based annotations.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_gating_strategy_fmc63_plot

celltypes_plot <- grep(
  "CD",

)

y_lines <- c(0.5, 1, 1.75, 2, 3)

p_list <- lapply(markers_plot, function(m) {
  p <- DensityScatterPlot(
    subset(pg_data, manual_cell_annotation %in% celltypes_plot),
    pt_size = 0.5,

})

p
```

The populations are not entirely pure here, warranting us to apply a gating approach for classifying FMC63 status on the CD4 and CD8 T cells. Thresholds are decided based on the data as seen in the density scatter plots.

```{r}
#| label: data_processing_gating_strategy_fmc63_plot_v2

# Subset data to CD4 and CD8 T cells
pg_data_t <- subset(
  pg_data,
  subset = manual_cell_annotation %in% c("CD4 T", "CD8 T", "T other")
)

# Classify CD4 cells into subtypes
t_cell_data <- FetchData(
  pg_data_t,
  vars = c("CD3e", "CD4", "CD8", "FMC63", "timepoint")
)

# pg_data_t was only needed to pull the marker values above
rm(pg_data_t)
gc()

# DECISION POINT.
# Define subtypes based on marker expression thresholds
# Adjust thresholds based on your data distribution
cutoff_cd3 <- 1.5
cutoff_cd4 <- 1
cutoff_cd8 <- 2
cutoff_fmc_t0 <- 2 # cutoff at 2 works best for b1, cutoff at 1.75 would be best for b2, but aiming for the stricter cutoff.
cutoff_fmc_t1 <- 0.5

tcell_classification <-
  t_cell_data |>
  mutate(
    tcell_subtype_broad = case_when(
      CD3e > cutoff_cd3 &
        CD4 > cutoff_cd4 &
        CD8 < cutoff_cd8 ~ "CD4 T",
      CD3e > cutoff_cd3 &
        CD4 < cutoff_cd4 &
        CD8 > cutoff_cd8 ~ "CD8 T",
      CD3e < cutoff_cd3 ~ "other",
      TRUE ~ "T other"
    )
  )

tcell_classification <-
  tcell_classification |>
  mutate(
    tcell_subtype = case_when(
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD4 T" &
        timepoint == "t0" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 ~ "CD4 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD4 T" &
        timepoint == "t1" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 ~ "CD4 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD8 T" &
        timepoint == "t0" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 ~ "CD8 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD8 T" &
        timepoint == "t1" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 ~ "CD8 T FMC63+",
      TRUE ~ tcell_subtype_broad
    )
  )

tcell_classification$tcell_subtype <- ifelse(
  tcell_classification$tcell_subtype %in% c("CD4 T", "CD8 T"),
  paste0(tcell_classification$tcell_subtype, " FMC63-"),
  tcell_classification$tcell_subtype
)

# Add subtype annotation to pg_data
pg_data$tcell_subtype <- pg_data$manual_cell_annotation
pg_data$tcell_subtype[rownames(
  tcell_classification
)] <- tcell_classification$tcell_subtype

# Add a column for FMC63 status alone in T cells
fmc_status <-
  t_cell_data |>
  mutate(
    tcell_fmc = case_when(
      FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 & timepoint == "t0" ~ "FMC63+",
      FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 & timepoint == "t1" ~ "FMC63+",
      TRUE ~ "FMC63-"
    )
  )

# Object-wide column: every cell starts as "FMC63-" and only the gated T cells
# are overwritten below. Non-T cells (myeloid, NK, platelets) are therefore
# "FMC63-" by construction rather than by gating - they are not CAR-expressing
# populations, but they were never tested against the FMC63 cutoffs.
pg_data$tcell_fmc_status <- "FMC63-"
pg_data$tcell_fmc_status[rownames(fmc_status)] <- fmc_status$tcell_fmc

# Bring NK cell annotation from l1 annotation
pg_data@meta.data <- pg_data@meta.data |>
  mutate(
    tcell_subtype = case_when(
      tcell_subtype == "other" & l1_annotation == "NK" ~ "NK",
      TRUE ~ tcell_subtype
    )
  )

# Visualize FMC64 T cell types on UMAP
DimPlot(
  pg_data,
  group.by = "tcell_subtype",
  cols = cell_type_palette_fmc,
  reduction = "harmony_umap"
) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  labs(title = "T Cell FMC63 status on UMAP")

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/gating_strategy/tcell_fmc_umap"
  ),
  width = 8,
  height = 6
)
```

## 2.7. Reprocess filtered object

### Platelet segmentation and clean-up

Identify platelet profile by computing weights to different protein markers. Set it against T cell population for better contrasts.
This module only computes and exports the weight matrix (and the platelet / T cell labels used to compute it). The actual clean up is run in the separate module `02b_platelet_cleanup.qmd`.

Steps:
1. calculate protein weights for platelets and t cells (in this script. save to r object `platelet_tcell_protein_weights.rds`)
2. subset data to only t cells (cd4 and cd8) and load cell graphs (done in batches in `02b_platelet_cleanup.qmd`)
3. segment cells based on assigned weights to identify platelets. Include interface to expand borders a bit and avoid excessive bleedover (`02b`)
4. Compute % of platelet nodes per cell and apply a filter to remove cells with too high platelet fraction (`02b`)
5. Remove the segmented platelet patches and interfacing nodes from each cell (`02b`)
6. For the remaining cells: (1) recompute protein abundance (`partition_counts()`) --> abundance matrix, (2) recompute proximity scores (`ComputeProximityScores(mode = "analytical")`) for cell graph list --> proximity table (`02b`)
7. Create a new PNA assay with the proximity scores (`tbl_df`) and count data (`02b`)

```{r}
DimPlot(pg_data, group.by = "seurat_clusters")

# Decision checkpoint: platelet clusters are specific to each clustering run
# (in pna_b1b2 they were clusters 1 and 5). Here they are chosen data-driven:
#   1. candidate clusters: >= 50% of cells labelled "Platelets" (reference
#      transfer). This alone is not specific enough, since clusters that mix
#      platelet-like and myeloid profiles can carry the same label.
#   2. platelet score per cluster: mean CLR of the core platelet markers.
#   3. platelet clusters: candidates above the largest gap in the sorted
#      cluster scores (no hand-set cutoff).
# Inspect the table below and overwrite `platelet_clusters` manually if needed.
platelet_score_markers <- c("CD41", "CD62P", "CD36", "CD9")
platelet_score_markers <- intersect(platelet_score_markers, rownames(pg_data))

platelet_clr <- SeuratObject::LayerData(pg_data, layer = "data")[
  platelet_score_markers,
  ,
  drop = FALSE
]
cluster_platelet_score <- pg_data@meta.data |>
  mutate(
    cell_platelet_score = Matrix::colMeans(platelet_clr[,
      rownames(pg_data@meta.data),
      drop = FALSE
    ])
  ) |>
  summarise(
    n_cells = n(),
    fraction_labelled_platelets = mean(tcell_subtype == "Platelets"),
    platelet_score = mean(cell_platelet_score),
    .by = seurat_clusters
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(platelet_score))

# Largest gap between consecutive scores; clusters above it have a high score
score_gaps <- -diff(cluster_platelet_score$platelet_score)
n_high <- which.max(score_gaps)
cluster_platelet_score <- cluster_platelet_score |>
  mutate(
    candidate = fraction_labelled_platelets >= 0.5,
    high_score = row_number() <= n_high,
    platelet_cluster = candidate & high_score
  )
print(cluster_platelet_score)

platelet_clusters <- cluster_platelet_score |>
  filter(platelet_cluster) |>
  pull(seurat_clusters) |>
  as.character()
message("Platelet clusters used: ", paste(platelet_clusters, collapse = ", "))

pg_data$anno_platelet <- ifelse(
  pg_data$tcell_subtype == "Platelets" &
    as.character(pg_data$seurat_clusters) %in% platelet_clusters,
  "platelet",
  ifelse(
    pg_data$tcell_subtype %in%
      c(
        "CD8 T FMC63-",
        "CD8 T FMC63+",
        "CD4 T FMC63-",
        "CD4 T FMC63+",
        "T other"
      ),
    "tcell",
    "other"
  )
)

w <- cc_protein_weights(
  pg_data,
  group_by = "anno_platelet",
  population_1 = "tcell",
  population_2 = "platelet"
)

# Export data to be used by 02b_platelet_cleanup.qmd
save_checkpoint("prefilter_seurat_object.rds", pg_data)
save_checkpoint("cluster_platelet_score.rds", cluster_platelet_score)
save_checkpoint("platelet_tcell_protein_weights.rds", w)
```

The segmentation, platelet filtering and recomputation of counts and proximity scores for all T cells is run in batches in the separate module `02b_platelet_cleanup.qmd`, which produces a cleaned object (`pg_data_platelet_cleaned.rds`). A 100-cell test of this strategy was used to develop that module.

### 2.7.1. Filter, normalize, dim reduction

From the initial run of the analysis, we could see that a pure data-driven clustering approach resulted in very few T cells, especially CD8+ and FMC63+ T cells, in some of the samples. Hence, we will instead try to do a more guided selection and annotation of the cell identities.

\(1\) In a first step, we can use the cell clustering results from above sections to label and exclude non-T cell populations. Especially platelets are of value to exclude from the downstream analysis. (2) Next, we will instead apply a marker gating strategy to label the different T cell population and FMC63 status.

**Step 1: Filter data**

First filter data to remove platelets and thereafter reprocess data (normalize and clustering)

```{r}
pg_data_filt <- pg_data |>
  subset(!tcell_subtype %in% c("Platelets", "other")) |>
  NormalizeData(normalization.method = "CLR", margin = 2) |>
  ScaleData()

n_pcs <- 50
n_dims <- 10
n_neighbors <- 30
pg_data_filt <-
  pg_data_filt |>
  RunPCA(npcs = n_pcs, features = selected_markers, seed.use = analysis_seed) |>
  RunUMAP(
    reduction = "pca",
    dims = 1:n_dims,
    n.neighbors = n_neighbors,
    seed.use = analysis_seed
  )

# Plot
ElbowPlot(pg_data_filt, ndims = 30)

cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data_filt,
    c(
      "sample_alias",
      "condition",
      "seurat_clusters",
      "manual_cell_annotation",
      "tcell_subtype"
    )
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

p1 <- Embeddings(pg_data_filt, "pca") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

p2 <- Embeddings(pg_data_filt, "umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = sample_alias)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = sample_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())

export_plot(
```

```{r}
pg_data_filt <- pg_data_filt |>
  RunHarmony(
    # condition is fully nested within sample_alias (each sample belongs to
    # exactly one condition), so harmonising per sample already removes all
    # condition-level structure. Matches the first RunHarmony call above.
    group.by.vars = "sample_alias",

    reduction = "harmony",
    dims = 1:n_dims,
    reduction.name = "harmony_umap",
    n.neighbors = n_neighbors,
    seed.use = analysis_seed
  )
```

### 2.7.2. Cluster and reannotate cells

```{r}
pg_data_filt <-
  pg_data_filt |>
  FindNeighbors(reduction = "harmony", dims = 1:n_dims) |>
  FindClusters(random.seed = analysis_seed, resolution = 0.5)

cell_metadata <-
  FetchData(pg_data_filt, c("sample_alias", "condition", "seurat_clusters")) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id")

Embeddings(pg_data_filt, "harmony_umap") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cell_id") |>
  left_join(cell_metadata, by = "cell_id") |>
  ggplot(aes(harmonyumap_1, harmonyumap_2, color = seurat_clusters)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5) +
  coord_fixed() +
  scale_color_manual(values = cluster_palette) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())


markers_of_interest <- c(
  "CD3e",
  "CD4",
  "CD8",
  "CD19",
  "CD14",
  "CD16",
  "CD56",

)

plot_data |>
```

**Step 2: Re-annotate cells clusters**

```{r}
#| label: filtered_data_processing_set_manual_annotation

# Annotation by label transfer
pg_data_filt <-
  pg_data_filt |>
  AnnotateCells(
    reference = reference,
    reference_groups = c("l1_annotation", "l2_annotation"),
    reference_assay = "PNA",
    query_assay = "PNA",
    # Summarise annotations by cluster, adding an extra column with majority vote
    summarize_by_column = "seurat_clusters",
    normalization_method = "CLR",
    method = "nmf"
  )

# Last use of the PBMC reference - free it before the rest of the module
rm(reference)
gc()

# Inspect the automatic annotation results to inform manual annotation

# while `l1_annotation_summary` and `l2_annotation_summary` contain the majority vote annotation per cluster

# This plot shows the distribution of automatic annotations across clusters,
# which can help to identify which clusters correspond to which cell types,
# and to identify whether the clustering resolves all cell identities of interest.

# Cell counts per cluster
table(pg_data_filt$seurat_clusters, pg_data_filt$l1_annotation) %>%
  ComplexHeatmap::pheatmap(
    .,

  as.ggplot()

  ),
  width = 10,
  height = 6
)

table(pg_data_filt$seurat_clusters, pg_data_filt$l2_annotation) %>%
  ComplexHeatmap::pheatmap(
    .,
    color = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry"),
    display_numbers = ifelse(. == 0, "", .),
    cellwidth = 16,
    cellheight = 8,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "Number of cells")
  ) |>
  as.ggplot()
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/cluster_vs_automatic_annotation/filtered_cluster_vs_l2_annotation_counts"
  ),
  width = 12,
  height = 6
)

table(pg_data_filt$seurat_clusters, pg_data_filt$l1_annotation_summary) %>%
  sweep(1, rowSums(.), FUN = "/") %>%
  `*`(100) %>% # Multiply by 100
  round(1) %>%
  ComplexHeatmap::pheatmap(
    .,
    color = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry"),
    display_numbers = ifelse(. == 0, "", .),
    cellwidth = 16,
    cellheight = 8,
    heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "% of cells")
  ) |>
  as.ggplot()
export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/cluster_vs_automatic_annotation/filtered_cluster_vs_l1_annotation_summary_percent"
  ),
  width = 10,
  height = 6

# Specify cell annotation labels for each cluster
# (These are example annotations and should be changed according to your dataset)
cell_anno_df_filt <- table(
  pg_data_filt$seurat_clusters,
  pg_data_filt$l1_annotation_summary # DECISION POINT: select level to base annotation on
) %>%
  sweep(1, rowSums(.), FUN = "/") %>%
  `*`(100) %>% # Multiply by 100
  round(1)

# As in section 2.6.4: this requires every cluster row to be 100% one label,
# which holds for the *_annotation_summary columns (per-cluster majority vote).
n_hits_filt <- apply(cell_anno_df_filt, 1, function(x) sum(x == 100))
if (any(n_hits_filt != 1)) {
  stop(
    "Expected exactly one 100% annotation per cluster, but cluster(s) ",
    paste(rownames(cell_anno_df_filt)[n_hits_filt != 1], collapse = ", "),
    " matched ",
    paste(n_hits_filt[n_hits_filt != 1], collapse = ", "),
    ". Use an *_annotation_summary column, which is constant within a cluster."
  )
}

cluster_cell_annotation <- setNames(
  colnames(cell_anno_df_filt)[apply(cell_anno_df_filt, 1, function(x) {
    which(x == 100)
  })],
  rownames(cell_anno_df_filt)
)

# NOTE: recode() drops names, so the setNames() below is load-bearing - it
# re-attaches the cluster ids by position. Do not remove it.
cluster_cell_annotation <- cluster_cell_annotation |>
  recode(
    "CD4 TEM" = "CD4 T",
    "Naive CD4 T" = "CD4 T",
    "CD8 TCM" = "CD8 T",
    "Naive CD8 T" = "CD8 T",
    "Classical Mono" = "Myeloid",
    "Non-classical Mono" = "Myeloid",
    "Mono" = "Myeloid",
    "DC" = "Myeloid",
    "CD56dim NK" = "NK",
    "Treg" = "T other",
    "gdT" = "T other"
  ) |>
  setNames(nm = rownames(cell_anno_df_filt))

# Add annotation to Seurat object
pg_data_filt[[]] <-
  pg_data_filt[[]] |>
  mutate(
    manual_cell_annotation_filt = cluster_cell_annotation[as.character(
      seurat_clusters
    )]
  )
```

Add marker gating for T cells

```{r}
#| label: filtered_data_processing_gating_strategy_tcells

# Classify CD4 cells into subtypes
t_cell_data <- FetchData(
  subset(pg_data_filt, !manual_cell_annotation_filt %in% c("Myeloid")),
  vars = c("CD3e", "CD4", "CD8", "FMC63", "donor", "timepoint")
)

# DECISION POINT. As in section 2.6.6 except for cutoff_cd8, raised from 2 to 2.5
# Define subtypes based on marker expression thresholds
# Adjust thresholds based on your data distribution
cutoff_cd3 <- 1.5
cutoff_cd4 <- 1
cutoff_cd8 <- 2.5 # CHANGED: in this data, we can increase this threshold to get cleaner CD8 T cells
cutoff_fmc_t0 <- 2 # cutoff at 2 works best for b1, cutoff at 1.75 would be best for b2, but aiming for the stricter cutoff.
cutoff_fmc_t1 <- 0.5 # Keep these the same as before

tcell_classification <-
  t_cell_data |>
  mutate(
    tcell_subtype_broad = case_when(
      CD3e > cutoff_cd3 &
        CD4 > cutoff_cd4 &
        CD8 < cutoff_cd8 ~ "CD4 T",
      CD3e > cutoff_cd3 &
        CD4 < cutoff_cd4 &
        CD8 > cutoff_cd8 ~ "CD8 T",
      CD3e < cutoff_cd3 ~ "other",
      TRUE ~ "T other"
    )
  )

tcell_classification <-
  tcell_classification |>
  mutate(
    tcell_subtype_filt = case_when(
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD4 T" &
        timepoint == "t0" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 ~ "CD4 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD4 T" &
        timepoint == "t1" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 ~ "CD4 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD8 T" &
        timepoint == "t0" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 ~ "CD8 T FMC63+",
      tcell_subtype_broad == "CD8 T" &
        timepoint == "t1" &
        FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 ~ "CD8 T FMC63+",
      TRUE ~ tcell_subtype_broad
    )
  )

tcell_classification$tcell_subtype_filt <- ifelse(
  tcell_classification$tcell_subtype_filt %in% c("CD4 T", "CD8 T"),
  paste0(tcell_classification$tcell_subtype_filt, " FMC63-"),
  tcell_classification$tcell_subtype_filt
)

# Add subtype annotation to pg_data
pg_data_filt$tcell_subtype_filt <- pg_data_filt$manual_cell_annotation_filt
pg_data_filt$tcell_subtype_filt[rownames(
  tcell_classification
)] <- tcell_classification$tcell_subtype_filt

# Add a column for FMC63 status alone in T cells
fmc_status <-
  t_cell_data |>
  mutate(
    tcell_fmc = case_when(
      FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t0 & timepoint == "t0" ~ "FMC63+",
      FMC63 > cutoff_fmc_t1 & timepoint == "t1" ~ "FMC63+",
      TRUE ~ "FMC63-"
    )
  )

# As above: "FMC63-" is the default for every cell, and only gated T cells are
# overwritten. Non-T cells are negative by construction, not by gating.
pg_data_filt$tcell_fmc_status <- "FMC63-"
pg_data_filt$tcell_fmc_status[rownames(fmc_status)] <- fmc_status$tcell_fmc


# Reannotate NK cells and myeloid cells
pg_data_filt@meta.data <- pg_data_filt@meta.data |>
  mutate(
    updated_cell_annotations_filt = case_when(
      tcell_subtype_filt %in%
        c("other", "T other") &
        manual_cell_annotation_filt == "NK" ~ "NK",
      tcell_subtype_filt %in%
        c("other") &
        manual_cell_annotation_filt == "Myeloid" ~ "Myeloid",
      TRUE ~ tcell_subtype_filt
    )
  )

# Visualize FMC64 T cell types on UMAP
DimPlot(
  pg_data_filt,
  group.by = "updated_cell_annotations_filt",
  cols = cell_type_palette_fmc,
  reduction = "harmony_umap"
) +
  theme(aspect.ratio = 1) +
  labs(title = "T Cell FMC63 status on UMAP")

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/annotation_plots/gating_strategy/filtered_data_tcell_fmc_umap"
  ),
```

### 2.7.4. Choose a cell annotation to use

> **Decision checkpoint** (which labels drive modules `03`–`05`)\
> This analysis sets `cell_annotation = manual_cell_gating_filt`, the gating-based labels built in section 2.7. The automatic PBMC label transfer (`l1_annotation_summary` / `l2_annotation_summary`) is retained only as supporting evidence, not as the annotation of record.

Three annotations were produced above: automatic label transfer against the PBMC reference, cluster-based manual labels, and marker gating. We now choose which one drives modules `03`–`05`.

We proceed with the **gating-based** annotation. Data-driven clustering did not separate the FMC63⁺ populations cleanly — the CAR⁺ cells do not form their own clusters at this resolution — so cluster labels alone cannot resolve the CD4/CD8 × FMC63 status distinction this study depends on. Marker gating on CD3e, CD4, CD8 and FMC63 (with timepoint-specific FMC63 cutoffs) does resolve it. Automatic label transfer still supplies the NK and myeloid assignments, and the cluster-based labels were used upstream to exclude platelets before reprocessing.

```{r}

  mutate(
    # Gating-based labels from section 2.7 (CD4/CD8 x FMC63 status, with NK and
    # myeloid carried over from the automatic annotation). To fall back to the

    cell_annotation = manual_cell_gating_filt
```

### 2.7.5. Marker selection per cell type

> **Decision checkpoint** (which markers enter differential testing)\
> The PLS and filter logic below defines `markers_to_test` for modules `04`–`05`. Adjust `isotype_markers` if your panel differs (defaults are mouse isotypes; use your human isotype controls for human panels). Review the scatter plot and heatmaps before trusting exclusions.

When later performing statistical tests, we want to guide our attention to markers that are more likely to be truly positive signals rather than markers than show background signal. For a given cell type, e.g. CD4 T cells, we can assume that most B cell markers should not be present. Therefore, we want to identify markers that are mostly associated with background signal across each cell type, so that we can disregard them in downstream analyses.

To identify such markers, we employ Partial Least Squares (PLS) regression, which allows us to model the relationship between isotype marker abundance and overall background signal in the dataset. The analysis is conducted separately for each cell type, allowing us to capture cell type-specific background patterns. The PLS model is fitted using isotype markers as predictors, and results in a background score describing the background level in each cell. Additionally, we obtain background loadings that indicate the contribution of each marker to the background signal. If a marker has a positive loading, it suggests that the marker is strongly associated with background signal in that cell type. For each cell type, we keep markers that either have a very high abundance (mean CLR \> 10 isotype CLR std) or have medium abundance (mean CLR \> 3 isotype CLR std) and a background PLS loading below 0.05. The markers that are retained in any condition will be used for downstream statistical testing.

We utilize the `isotype_pls` helper function to perform the PLS regression. The function takes as input the isotype markers, a model matrix to account for sample-level covariates, and options to specify the data layer and whether to remove covariate effects. The output includes both the background scores for each cell and the loadings for each marker.

```{r}
#| label: statistical_testing_marker_selection

cell_annotation_column <-
  "cell_annotation"
isotype_markers <-
  c("mIgG1", "mIgG2a", "mIgG2b")
minimum_cell_count <- 2 # Minimum number of cells per sample to include in statistical testing

cell_data <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data,
    vars = c(cell_annotation_column, "sample_alias")
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  group_by(cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column))

# Keep cell types present in ≥2 samples with enough cells per sample
# (single-sample cell types make model.matrix(~ factor(sample_alias)) intercept-only)
#
# NOTE: sample_alias is a factor over all samples, so table(sample_alias) counts
# every level - including the ones this cell type is absent from, which come back
# as 0. Without droplevels() the filter therefore demands presence in *every*
# sample, not in >=2, and silently drops any cell type missing from even one.
cell_data <-
  cell_data %>%
  filter(
    n_distinct(sample_alias) >= 2,
    min(table(droplevels(sample_alias))) >= minimum_cell_count
  )

if (nrow(cell_data) == 0) {
  stop(
    "No cell types remain for isotype background scoring after filtering ",
    "(need >=2 samples with at least ",
    minimum_cell_count,
    " cells each). ",
    "Lower minimum_cell_count or check cell_annotation / sample composition."
  )
}

pls_fit_celltype <-
  cell_data |>
  group_split() |>
  set_names(group_keys(cell_data)$cell_type) |>
  lapply(function(cells) {
    pg_data |>
      subset(cells = cells$component) %>%
      isotype_pls(
        isotype_markers,
        model_mat = with(
          .[[]],
          model.matrix(~ factor(sample_alias))
        ),
        layer = "data",
        remove_covariates = TRUE
      )
  })


# Background scores
bg_scores <-
  pls_fit_celltype |>
  lapply(function(x) enframe(x$scores, "component", "bg_score")) |>
  bind_rows()

pg_data[[]] <-
  pg_data[[]] |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  left_join(bg_scores, by = "component") |>
  column_to_rownames("component")


FeaturePlot(
  pg_data,
  features = "bg_score",
  reduction = "harmony_umap"
) +
  scale_color_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry")) +
  labs(title = "Isotype background score")

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_score_featureplot"
  ),
  width = 6,
  height = 5
)

# Background loadings

bg_loadings <-
  pls_fit_celltype %>%
  lapply(function(x) enframe(x$loadings, "marker", "bg_loading")) |>
  bind_rows(.id = cell_annotation_column)

bg_loadings |>
  arrange(-bg_loading) |>
  mutate(marker = factor(marker, levels = unique(marker))) |>
  ggplot(aes(marker, !!sym(cell_annotation_column), fill = bg_loading)) +
  geom_tile() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1)
  ) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "BluesCherry")) +
  labs(
    title = "PLS loadings for isotype markers",
    x = "Marker",
    fill = "PLS loading",
    y = "Cell type"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_loading_heatmap"
  ),
  width = 15,
  height = 6
)


FetchData(pg_data, vars = isotype_markers, layer = "data") |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  left_join(bg_scores, by = c("component")) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(isotype_markers),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(abundance, bg_score)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") +
  geom_text(
    data = . %>%
      group_by(marker) %>%
      summarise(cor = cor(abundance, bg_score)),
    aes(label = paste0("r = ", round(cor, 2))),
    x = Inf,
    y = -Inf,
    hjust = 1.1,
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 3
  ) +
  facet_grid(~marker, scales = "free_x") +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Background score vs isotype marker abundance",
    x = "Marker abundance (CLR)",
    y = "Background score"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/isotype_background_score_vs_isotype_abundance"
  ),
  width = 12,
  height = 5
)

isotype_levels <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data,
    c(
      "condition",
      cell_annotation_column,
      isotype_markers
    )
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  mutate(max_isotype = pmax(!!!syms(isotype_markers))) |>
  group_by(condition, !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  summarise(
    mean_isotype = mean(max_isotype),
    sd_isotype = sd(max_isotype)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

abundance_data_per_celltype <-
  FetchData(
    pg_data,
    c(
      "condition",
      cell_annotation_column,
      rownames(pg_data)
    )
  ) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "component") |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = all_of(rownames(pg_data)),
    names_to = "marker",
    values_to = "abundance"
  ) |>
  group_by(condition, !!sym(cell_annotation_column), marker) |>
  summarise(
    mean_abundance = mean(abundance),
    sd_abundance = sd(abundance),
    n_cells = n()
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  left_join(
    isotype_levels,
    by = c(
      "condition",
      cell_annotation_column
    )
  ) |>
  left_join(
    bg_loadings,
    by = c(
      "marker",
      cell_annotation_column
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    is_low = mean_abundance < mean_isotype + 3 * sd_isotype,
    is_high = mean_abundance > mean_isotype + 10 * sd_isotype,
    # A cell type filtered out above has no PLS loadings, so bg_loading is NA
    # here. case_when treats an NA condition as "no match" and falls through to
    # the TRUE branch, which means such markers would silently pass on abundance
    # alone. Make that explicit rather than implicit.
    no_bg_model = is.na(bg_loading),
    is_noisy = coalesce(bg_loading > 0.05, FALSE),
    passed_filter = case_when(
      is_low ~ "Not passed",
      is_high ~ "Passed",
      is_noisy ~ "Not passed",
      TRUE ~ "Passed"
    ),
    # Display-only refinement of passed_filter: keeps the pass/fail decision
    # above unchanged while making the unmodelled markers visible in the plot.
    filter_status = case_when(
      passed_filter == "Passed" & no_bg_model ~ "Passed (no background model)",
      TRUE ~ passed_filter
    )
  )

# Flag any cell type that was scored without a background model
cell_types_without_bg_model <-
  abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  filter(no_bg_model) |>
  pull(!!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  unique()

if (length(cell_types_without_bg_model) > 0) {
  message(
    "No isotype background model for: ",
    paste(cell_types_without_bg_model, collapse = ", "),
    ". Markers for these cell types were selected on abundance alone ",
    "(no bg_loading filter). They were excluded by the sample/cell-count ",
    "filter above - lower minimum_cell_count to include them."
  )
}

abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  mutate(cell_annotation = !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  ggplot(aes(
    (mean_abundance - mean_isotype) / sd_isotype,
    bg_loading,
    color = filter_status
  )) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  geom_point(size = 0.1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = marker), size = 2) +
  facet_grid(condition ~ cell_annotation) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(
    title = "Marker mean abundance vs PLS loading",
    x = "Mean abundance (CLR)",
    y = "PLS loading"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/marker_selection_scatterplot"
  ),
  width = 15,
  height = 10
)

markers_per_cell_type <-
  abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  filter(passed_filter == "Passed") |>
  select(condition, cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column), marker) |>
  distinct() |>
  group_by(cell_type)

abundance_data_per_celltype |>
  mutate(cell_type = !!sym(cell_annotation_column)) |>
  filter(passed_filter == "Passed") |>
  ggplot(aes(marker, condition)) +
  geom_tile() +
  facet_grid(cell_type ~ .) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colors = PixelgenGradient(100, "Cherry")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust = 1),
    panel.background = element_rect(fill = "white"),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Selected markers per cell type",
    x = "Marker",
    y = "Condition"
  )

export_plot(
  filename = here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/selected_markers_heatmap"
  ),
  width = 12,
  height = 8
)

markers_per_cell_type |>
  write_csv(here::here(
    "pna_3",
    "results/02_clustering_annotation/isotype_background_score/selected_markers.csv"
  ))

markers_to_test <-
  markers_per_cell_type |>
  group_split() |>
  set_names(group_keys(markers_per_cell_type)$cell_type) |>
  lapply(function(df) unique(df$marker))
```

```{r}
save_checkpoint("annotated_seurat_object.rds", pg_data)
save_checkpoint("markers_to_test.rds", markers_to_test)
```
